chapters.title: The app on my laptop
summary: Today the app lives in your own house: web, api, Postgres and Redis in Docker, plus a one-off migrate job.
Every laptop piece has a twin on AWS. The pencil outlines are the city we will build, chapter by chapter.
On AWS every connection must pass three checks: Reach (roads and guards), Allowed (badges), Password (keys).

chapters.title: AWS basics
summary: We own land (the account) in a country (region us-east-1) with two districts (AZs us-east-1a and us-east-1b).
Pulumi, the city planner, builds from our code and keeps a record book (the state) in Pulumi Cloud.
Every building gets name plates (tags), and the treasurer (a $20 budget) emails us before the bill hurts.

chapters.title: The network (VPC)
summary: Our private city minitickets-dev-vpc (10.0.0.0/16): two neighborhoods on the main road, two behind walls.
One city gate (minitickets-dev-igw). The road sign public-rt sends 0.0.0.0/0 to it; private-rt only knows the city.
"Public" is only what the road sign says. No NAT gateway: it would cost more than everything else together.

chapters.title: Security groups
summary: The roads exist. Guards now decide which building door accepts which visitor.

ALB reaches web:3000 and API:4000; API reaches DB:5432 and Valkey:6379. Rules reference source groups rather than changing task IPs. SGs are stateful; a route and an allowed port are separate requirements.
A task can have a route and still time out at a closed building door. Compare source SG, destination port and task ENI before blaming the password.

chapters.title: Public IPs and network interfaces
summary: A worker needs an address as well as a guest-list entry.

Fargate awsvpc gives each task an ENI with private address and attached groups. Public-subnet tasks use a public IP for outbound image/secrets access; that does not open inbound ports. Private data has no public entry. No NAT gateway is built.
A public subnet alone does not give a worker internet access. Check route, public-IP assignment and egress; public IPv4 and NAT have different running costs.

chapters.title: The database and cache
summary: Workers need durable records and a shared short-term memory behind the walls.

Postgres is the booking source of truth; Valkey holds sessions, cached event lists, token buckets and advisory inventory. A cache may evict data; SQL transactions and CHECK/unique constraints still protect seats. Data switches and retained backups are independent of compute.

Follow the API ENI to private data subnets. Reach means route + SG, Allowed means the relevant service policy where used, Password means DB/Redis credentials and TLS. Never test by printing secret values.

chapters.title: Secrets
summary: The worker needs a key safe, not passwords written on its name plate.

RDS manages the DB master secret; Valkey/revalidation/origin/signing secrets have distinct purposes and permissions. ECS execution roles inject selected secret fields at task start; application roles fetch only what runtime code needs. Secret ARNs are not secret values.

A task can reach the safe but lack its badge, or have a badge and use the wrong secret field. Rotation needs coordinated credentials and consumer restart/key-ring behavior; automatic ticket key rotation is not built.

chapters.title: ECR
summary: Workers must fetch an immutable packed app from the warehouse.

API, web and worker have separate repositories. Publish builds a git-SHA image once per service, then deployment uses that tag through SSM. Lifecycle policies preserve deployed/recent artifacts; latest is not the release authority. No registry password is committed.
A successful push does not mean a task can pull. Compare image URI/architecture, execution-role ECR permissions and network egress.

chapters.title: ECS
summary: A manager must keep the right packed workers running and replace unhealthy ones.

Fargate arm64 tasks run API and web as separate services; task definitions pin image/env/secrets/roles. Readiness checks data dependencies; liveness only proves a process answers. A dedicated minitickets-dev-migrate task applies SQL before rollout, not inside every API task.
A stopped task has a stoppedReason, exit code and log stream. A service Event often explains image-pull, secret, ENI or health-check failures faster than restarting it.

chapters.title: IAM roles
summary: The manager, workers and publisher need different staff badges.

Trust says who may assume a role; permissions say which actions on which resource ARNs; attachment says which task/function/job uses it. ECS execution roles pull/log/inject secrets; the API task role publishes SNS, queries tickets and signs constrained S3 access; Lambda roles receive their own queue and touch their own outputs.
AccessDenied is not a network timeout. Identify the caller ARN and denied action/resource, inspect trust and permission separately, then check attached taskRoleArn vs executionRoleArn.

chapters.title: The ALB
summary: Visitors need one HTTPS reception desk that sends pages and API calls to healthy staff.

ACM validates minitickets.theversehub.in; HTTPS listener routes /trpc/* to API and other paths to web. Target groups track health independently. ALB-only mode accepts the owner-selected source CIDRs; the committed cdnEnabled=false remains the current shape.
A 502/503 can mean no healthy targets, wrong container port or an application crash. Check listener rule, target health reason, task health and logs in that order.

chapters.title: Service Connect
summary: Web server rendering needs the API without going back through public reception.

Service Connect exposes api/web names via task-local proxies (API proxy 14000, web proxy 13000). API_INTERNAL_URL is server-only; browser requests still use the public /trpc route. Proxy port ingress differs from the application container port.
A browser can work while SSR fails. Check the internal name, Service Connect discovery and proxy SG rule. Localhost-originated internal calls are not trusted for forged X-Forwarded-For.

chapters.title: CloudFront
summary: An optional front layer can bring static files closer to visitors.

CloudFront is implemented but currently inactive: cdnEnabled=false pending account verification. Static assets can be cached; private/RSC/API answers cannot. P10 nonce-bearing HTML is now private,no-store; the events policy min/default TTL 0 honors it. Origin protection uses a secret header and AWS prefix-list mode when enabled.
Do not claim an inactive distribution is live. First diagnose the ALB path; then compare behavior, cache key, origin headers, DNS and certificate region.

chapters.title: CI/CD
summary: A publisher needs a short-lived badge and a deployment record, not laptop keys.

GitHub OIDC trust restricts repository/environment subjects. CI checks code/tests/audit and Trivy images; publish builds SHA artifacts once; approved deploy records the tag in SSM, migrates, then rolls services/Lambdas. Guards reject stale infrastructure code and superseded approved runs.

An old approved run must not delete newer resources. Distinguish app rollback (old image/current infra) from infra rollback and an additive migration; never locally overwrite the SSM release parameter.

chapters.title: Queues, DLQs and SNS fan-out
summary: Booking commits need two durable consumers without losing messages between SQL and delivery.

The API commits confirmation payload in a Postgres outbox with the booking. A relay publishes to SNS; raw subscriptions copy the event into separate jobs and tickets SQS queues, each with a DLQ/redrive policy. One consumer failure does not block the other.
SNS is fan-out, SQS is durable backlog and retry, the outbox closes the commit/publish gap. A relay can publish twice after an unknown acknowledgement; consumers must be idempotent.

chapters.title: Lambda workers
summary: Queue messages need workers that scale independently from the API.

Email Lambda is 256 MB / 10 s; ticket Lambda is 512 MB / 30 s. Both use the published worker image with different commands. Event-source mappings use partial batch failure responses. They do not need the VPC because their stores are managed AWS APIs, not RDS.

Visibility timeout must outlast processing/retry behavior; partial failure reports only failed message identifiers. Whole-batch failure replays successful siblings; concurrency limits can cause throttling/redrive.

chapters.title: DynamoDB records
summary: Consumers need durable dedupe and owner/date access patterns without an SQL connection pool.

Processed jobs use jobKey plus TTL. Ticket rows use userId/ticketId and by-event-date GSI for a future reminder path. Conditional writes reserve canonical ticket work and support idempotent repair; owner Query is strongly consistent, GSI reads are not. TTL is asynchronous cleanup, not an authorization clock.
Design keys from reads before writing rows. A hot date partition, eventual GSI propagation and duplicate delivery are different failure modes; Query differs from scanning the whole table.

chapters.title: SES delivery
summary: A confirmed booking needs an email delivery service with a verified sender.

SES identity/DKIM records prove sender ownership. Sandbox delivery requires verified recipients and is quota-limited; first AWS delivery remains acceptance work. Lambda IAM restricts sender identities and From address. Provider acceptance is not an exactly-once inbox guarantee.
If SES accepted but the consumer crashed before marking done, retry can send twice. DKIM improves authentication, not universal inbox placement; production access/quota is separate from IAM.

chapters.title: Private S3 assets and signed tickets
summary: A ticket needs a private QR artifact and a short-lived way for its owner to read it.

Bucket ownership/public-access block, SSE-S3 and TLS-only policy protect assets. HMAC signs ticket claims; deterministic seat keys plus conditional Dynamo rows converge under duplicates. API owner-scopes reads and issues 120-second GET/download capabilities. Admin poster PUTs are constrained, staged, byte-checked and copied immutably; CORS is not authorization.
Never log raw signed URLs or signing values. MIME/header checks are not malware scanning/full decoding. Scanner verification/redemption and automated key-ring rotation are explain-only, not shipped.

chapters.title: Alarms and observability
summary: The city diary must show one booking across API and consumers and call for help when backlog grows.

Correlation ids flow through request logs, outbox payload, SNS/SQS and Lambda JSON. CloudWatch alarms cover queue age, DLQ, worker errors/throttles; the dashboard combines metrics and saved queries. SNS email subscriptions need confirmation. Browser vitals are structured logs, not trusted billing data or custom metrics.
An alarm without confirmed email delivery is silent. Missing data policy, evaluation periods and age vs depth matter; search by correlation id before guessing which process failed.

chapters.title: Reminder scheduler (explain-only)
summary: A reminder the day before would branch from ticket date access into the existing email path.

Not built: a daily Scheduler would invoke a reminder Lambda, query tomorrow in by-event-date, and enqueue one email job per ticket/day. No VPC/RDS is needed. The Scheduler badge would trust scheduler.amazonaws.com and allow InvokeFunction on only that function.

Where it would go: a new infra/src/jobs/reminders.ts and apps/worker/src/reminders handler/service beside current workers. Conditional ticket/day dedupe and paginated/sharded date queries prevent duplicate or unbounded sends.

chapters.title: Door check-in (explain-only)
summary: The door would authenticate a QR and atomically consume it once.

Not built: REST API usage plans/API keys throttle staff devices, but are not staff authorization. A check-in Lambda would verify the HMAC then conditionally update valid→used in DynamoDB. Two scans race: one succeeds, one returns already-used time. A staff scanner would keep its key out of the bundle.

Where it would go: apps/web/src/features/checkin plus a check-in Lambda and infra/src/tickets/checkin.ts. HTTP API lacks REST usage-plan features; camera input is untrusted and a signed QR alone is replayable.

chapters.title: Autoscaling (explain-only)
summary: A manager could add workers when traffic grows, but workers cannot create more seats.

Not built: an ECS desired-count target, min 1/max 3, CPU or ALB requests-per-target policy and cost budget. P8 instead builds shared rate limiting and an advisory inventory gate; Postgres still enforces stock. Waiting room, queued booking and expiring customer seat holds are explain-only too.

Where it would go: a new infra/src/compute/autoscaling.ts after services/target groups. More tasks increase DB connections and contention; define a queue-depth/latency objective, cooldown and maximum spend before adding capacity.

chapters.title: Debugging playbook
summary: Follow the failed request through the city rather than restarting unrelated pieces.

Start at the observed symptom and correlation id. Reach checks DNS/routes/SG/ports; Allowed checks IAM caller/action/resource; Password checks secret field/version/TLS without printing values. Then inspect DB locks, pool timeouts, queue age, DLQ/error logs and release SHA.

Change one explanation at a time. A 403 is not fixed by opening a subnet; a lock wait is not fixed by rotating an S3 key. Reproduce in disposable local resources and distinguish local proof from AWS acceptance.

chapters.title: The final poster
summary: The whole city should fit in an explanation you can give without memorizing 100 service names.

Browser→ALB→web/API→Postgres/Valkey is the synchronous path. Booking→outbox→SNS→two SQS queues→Lambdas→SES or S3/DynamoDB is the side path. OIDC/ECR/SSM/CD changes versions. SGs govern reach, IAM grants actions, secrets prove identity. Optional CloudFront and explain-only features remain distinct.
Say which invariant each piece protects and which failure it cannot prevent. Then ask about traffic, latency, durability, privacy and budget before proposing another service.

decor.text: Made by AWS with every city:

components.name: web container (Next.js)
components.city: In your own house: the web room
components.what: Builds the pages. Port 3000 inside the container; your browser opens localhost:3100 (pnpm app:up).
components.why: It is the part visitors see. On AWS it becomes a worker, kept on shift by a manager.
settings: Port 3000 inside, published as localhost:3100
Calls the api server to server at http://api:4000 (API_INTERNAL_URL)
REVALIDATE_SECRET: the same value as the api's
components.console: Docker Desktop → Containers → web → column Port(s)
components.debug: The page loads but the events list fails: check that the api runs and that API_INTERNAL_URL points at it.
components.interview: Locally the web server reaches the api by Docker's name "api"; on AWS Service Connect gives it the same name.
components.twin: ECS service minitickets-dev-web and its task (chapter 8)

components.name: api container (Fastify + tRPC)
components.city: In your own house: the api room
components.what: Holds the rules and talks to Postgres and Redis. Port 4000 inside, localhost:4100 outside.
components.why: All server logic lives here. On AWS it becomes a worker in a public neighborhood, guarded so only the reception desk can call it.
settings: Port 4000 inside, published as localhost:4100
DATABASE_URL and REDIS_URL name the containers postgres and redis
Checks every setting at start and stops if one is missing (EnvSchema)
components.console: Docker Desktop → Containers → api → Logs
components.debug: "Invalid environment variables" at start: copy apps/api/.env.example to apps/api/.env and fill it in.
components.interview: The api validates its environment with Zod at startup, so a missing setting on AWS is one clear log line, not a strange bug later.
components.twin: ECS service minitickets-dev-api and its task (chapter 8)

components.name: migrate container
components.type: Docker container on the laptop (runs once)
components.city: In your own house: the builder who sets up the shelves once
components.what: Applies the SQL migrations, then exits. The api starts only after it succeeded.
components.why: If every api copy ran migrations at startup, they would race each other.
settings: command: node dist/migrate.js
restart "no": runs once and stays finished
The api waits for it (service_completed_successfully)
components.console: Docker Desktop → Containers → migrate (shown as exited: that is correct)
components.debug: The api never starts: migrate failed. Read its logs first.
components.interview: Migrations run as a separate one-off job before the new version starts, never inside the app's own startup.
components.twin: The migration task minitickets-dev-migrate, run by CD (chapter 13)

components.name: postgres container (Postgres 17.6)
components.city: In your own house: the filing cabinet
components.what: Keeps users and events. The data lives in the Docker volume postgres_data, so it survives a restart.
components.why: Our data must outlive every container. On AWS it moves behind the walls, where nobody outside can reach it.
settings: image postgres:17.6
port 5432
user and password from the root .env, inside DATABASE_URL
components.console: Docker Desktop → Containers → postgres
components.debug: "port is already allocated": another Postgres already uses 5432 on your machine.
components.interview: Locally Postgres is a container with a volume; on AWS it is RDS in private subnets, with an RDS-managed password in Secrets Manager.
components.twin: RDS Postgres 17 minitickets-dev-db, behind the walls (chapter 5)

components.name: redis container (Redis 7.4.5)
components.city: In your own house: the notepad by the door
components.what: Keeps sessions and a 30-second events cache.
components.why: Fast, short-lived data. On AWS it becomes Valkey, which speaks the same language.
settings: image redis:7.4.5
port 6379 inside (REDIS_PORT can move the laptop side)
maxmemory 256mb, evicts the least recently used keys
components.console: Docker Desktop → Containers → redis
components.cli: docker compose exec redis redis-cli ping
components.debug: Logins fail and the api logs Redis errors: is the redis container healthy?
components.interview: Sessions and the events cache live in Redis locally and in ElastiCache Valkey on AWS, over TLS (rediss://).
components.twin: ElastiCache Valkey 8.2 minitickets-dev-valkey, behind the walls (chapter 5)

components.name: Your AWS account
components.what: Our private space in AWS. Everything we build is registered to it, and the bills go to it.
components.why: Every AWS request is signed by someone in an account. It is the strongest wall AWS has between two setups.
settings: One account, dev only (there is no prod stack)
Locally you act through the CLI profile ticketlite
The 12-digit account ID is looked up by the code, never typed into it
components.console: Top right: your account name → the menu shows the Account ID
components.debug: "Your session has expired. Please reauthenticate using 'aws login'": run the login command it names. Wrong account? Check AWS_PROFILE.
components.interview: One account for dev. In a real company: separate accounts for dev, staging, prod and security, because an account is the strongest boundary.

components.name: us-east-1 (N. Virginia)
components.what: A geographic area of AWS data centres. Almost everything we build (the VPC, ECS, RDS, ECR, Secrets Manager) lives in this one region.
components.why: Things built in one region are invisible from another. Picking one region keeps all our pieces close together.
settings: us-east-1, shown as N. Virginia in the console
Set once in infra/Pulumi.dev.yaml (aws:region)
Global services (IAM, Budgets, CloudFront) sit outside any region
components.console: Top bar → the region selector shows N. Virginia (us-east-1)
components.debug: The console shows no VPC or a CLI command says "not found": you are looking at the wrong country. Switch to us-east-1.
components.interview: Resources are global, regional or zonal. We run everything regional in us-east-1, across two AZs.

components.name: us-east-1a
components.city: District A, with its own power supply
components.what: One isolated group of data centres in us-east-1. Home of public-1 and private-1.
components.why: If one district loses power, the other keeps going. The ALB and the RDS subnet group require at least two.
settings: Name us-east-1a: a label for OUR account (AWS shuffles names per account)
AZ ID use1-az1: the same building in every account
createNetwork takes the first two available AZs
components.console: VPC → Subnets → columns Availability Zone and Availability Zone ID
components.debug: Comparing two accounts? Compare AZ IDs, never AZ names.
components.interview: Two AZs is the cheapest shape the ALB and RDS accept. In dev only the shape is redundant: one copy of each stateful part.

components.name: us-east-1b
components.city: District B, with its own power supply
components.what: The second isolated group of data centres we use. Home of public-2 and private-2.
components.why: The second district is what lets the city survive a power cut in the first.
settings: Name us-east-1b (per account)
AZ ID use1-az2 (the same in every account)
createNetwork takes the first two available AZs
components.console: VPC → Subnets → columns Availability Zone and Availability Zone ID
components.debug: Comparing two accounts? Compare AZ IDs, never AZ names.
components.interview: Subnets are zonal: each lives in exactly one AZ. We put one public and one private subnet in each of the two.

components.name: Tags: Project, Env, ManagedBy, Name
components.what: Labels on every resource: Project=minitickets, Env=dev, ManagedBy=pulumi, and Name, which the console shows as the title.
components.why: To find our things, to split the bill by project, and to see which tool made a resource.
settings: commonTags: Project=minitickets, Env=dev, ManagedBy=pulumi
tagsFor(name) adds Name=<the name>
Route table associations carry no tags (AWS doesn't support them there)
To split the bill by tag, activate it in Billing → Cost allocation tags
components.console: Any resource → Tags tab. Resource Groups & Tag Editor → Tag Editor → region us-east-1, tag Project = minitickets → Search resources
components.debug: Something unknown costs money? Its tags say whose it is. No tags at all: probably not made by our Pulumi code.
components.interview: Every resource is named minitickets-dev-… and tagged by project, environment and tool, so ownership and cost are visible.

components.name: Pulumi stack dev
components.city: The city planner: a blueprint and a record book
components.what: Runs our TypeScript (infra/index.ts), compares it with its record book (the state, kept in Pulumi Cloud) and makes AWS match.
components.why: Nobody builds by clicking: every change is code, previewed before it happens, and the city can be rebuilt from scratch.
settings: Stack dev; its settings are in infra/Pulumi.dev.yaml
preview (read-only) → up (makes changes) → state → stack outputs
State in Pulumi Cloud, locked during an update
The on/off switches: dataEnabled, computeEnabled, entryEnabled, cdnEnabled
components.console: In infra/, run pulumi console → stack dev → Resources tab (and the Outputs on the overview page)
components.cli:
cd infra && pulumi preview
pulumi stack output
components.debug: A change made by clicking in the AWS console is invisible to preview: Pulumi compares with its record book. pulumi refresh reads AWS first.
components.interview: One function per layer, wired in index.ts; preview before every change; the state lives in Pulumi Cloud, which locks it during an update.

components.name: minitickets-dev-monthly-cost
components.what: A $20-a-month cost budget that emails us at 25%, 50% and 100% of real spend, and when AWS forecasts the month will pass 100%.
components.why: Cloud bills grow quietly. This is our smoke alarm. It only warns; it never stops anything.
settings: limitAmount "20" USD, MONTHLY
Alerts: 25, 50, 100% actual; 100% forecasted
includeCredit false: AWS credits don't hide the real cost
Email address from config alertEmail (stored encrypted)
components.console: Billing and Cost Management → Budgets → minitickets-dev-monthly-cost (amount $20.00, and the Alerts section)
components.debug: Billing data is hours late. An alert email means: find what is on, then turn the switches off (commit, push, approve).
components.interview: A $20 budget with 25/50/100% actual and a forecast alert, plus on/off switches for the hourly-billed layers.

components.name: The internet
components.city: The world outside the city wall
components.what: Every address that is not in our VPC. In a route table, 0.0.0.0/0 means "all of it".
components.why: Visitors come from here. Our workers also fetch images, secrets and send logs through it, to AWS's public endpoints.
settings: Reached only through the city gate (minitickets-dev-igw)
Only from neighborhoods whose road sign has 0.0.0.0/0 → igw
Only by things that have a public IP (chapter 4)
components.console: Nothing to open: look at the route tables that point at the gate
components.debug: Something can't reach the internet: check the four conditions (route, public IP, security group, something listening).
components.interview: 0.0.0.0/0 is the default route: it matches everything no more specific route matches.

components.name: minitickets-dev-vpc
components.what: Our own private network in AWS: 65,536 addresses (10.0.0.0/16) that only we use.
components.why: Every database, container and load balancer needs an address in a network. In a city of our own, nothing gets in unless we build a way.
settings: cidrBlock 10.0.0.0/16 (every address starting 10.0.)
enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames: true, so machines can look up names
AWS made with it: a main route table, a default network ACL and a default security group
components.console: VPC → Your VPCs → minitickets-dev-vpc → Details (IPv4 CIDR, DNS resolution, DNS hostnames) and the Resource map tab
components.debug: Not in the list? You are in the wrong region: switch to N. Virginia. The ID only changes if the network is deleted and built again.
components.interview: A /16 VPC across two AZs. Everything else lives inside it, which is why security groups and target groups need its ID.

components.name: minitickets-dev-igw
components.what: The only way between our VPC and the internet, in both directions. Attached to minitickets-dev-vpc.
components.why: Without it the city is sealed. On its own it does nothing: a road sign must point at it.
settings: vpcId: vpc.id attaches it to our VPC
Redundant and highly available: not inside one district
Translates between a resource's private address and its public IP
components.console: VPC → Internet gateways → minitickets-dev-igw → State: Attached, VPC ID
components.debug: A public thing is unreachable: is the gate Attached, and does the subnet's route table point at it?
components.interview: An internet gateway is a two-way door for things with public IPs; a NAT gateway is a one-way exit for private things.

components.name: minitickets-dev-public-1
components.city: A neighborhood on the main road
components.what: Addresses 10.0.0.0 to 10.0.0.255 in district us-east-1a. Its road sign, public-rt, leads to the city gate.
components.why: The reception desk (ALB) must be reachable from the internet, and our workers need a way out without a NAT gateway. Both live here.
settings: cidrBlock 10.0.0.0/24: 256 addresses, 251 usable
availabilityZone us-east-1a (use1-az1)
mapPublicIpOnLaunch true: things started here get a public IP
Associated with minitickets-dev-public-rt (public-rta-1)
components.console: VPC → Subnets → minitickets-dev-public-1 → Details: IPv4 CIDR, Availability Zone, Route table, Auto-assign public IPv4 address: Yes
components.debug: Behaves like a private subnet? Details → Route table must be minitickets-dev-public-rt, not the main route table.
components.interview: It is public only because its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the internet gateway. The name does nothing.

components.name: minitickets-dev-public-2
components.city: A neighborhood on the main road
components.what: Addresses 10.0.1.0 to 10.0.1.255 in district us-east-1b. Same road sign as public-1.
components.why: The ALB needs subnets in two districts, and a worker can start in either one.
settings: cidrBlock 10.0.1.0/24
availabilityZone us-east-1b (use1-az2)
mapPublicIpOnLaunch true
Associated with minitickets-dev-public-rt (public-rta-2)
components.console: VPC → Subnets → minitickets-dev-public-2 → Details
components.debug: Behaves differently from public-1? Compare Details → Route table and Auto-assign public IPv4 address.
components.interview: One public subnet per AZ, so the load balancer and the tasks can survive the loss of one AZ.

components.name: minitickets-dev-private-1
components.what: Addresses 10.0.10.0 to 10.0.10.255 in district us-east-1a. Its road sign, private-rt, knows only the city.
components.why: The database and the cache (chapter 5) live here: nobody outside should ever reach them.
settings: cidrBlock 10.0.10.0/24
availabilityZone us-east-1a (use1-az1)
mapPublicIpOnLaunch false: no public IPs
Associated with minitickets-dev-private-rt (private-rta-1)
components.console: VPC → Subnets → minitickets-dev-private-1 → Details: Route table minitickets-dev-private-rt, Auto-assign public IPv4 address: No
components.debug: Something here is reachable from the internet? Someone added 0.0.0.0/0 to private-rt. Remove it.
components.interview: Private means: no route to the internet gateway and no public IPs. The data stores live here.

components.name: minitickets-dev-private-2
components.what: Addresses 10.0.11.0 to 10.0.11.255 in district us-east-1b. Same road sign as private-1.
components.why: RDS and ElastiCache ask for subnets in at least two districts, even for a single database.
settings: cidrBlock 10.0.11.0/24
availabilityZone us-east-1b (use1-az2)
mapPublicIpOnLaunch false
Associated with minitickets-dev-private-rt (private-rta-2)
components.console: VPC → Subnets → minitickets-dev-private-2 → Details
components.debug: A subnet group refuses to be created with one subnet: it needs two districts.
components.interview: Two private subnets in two AZs, because the RDS subnet group demands two AZs.

components.name: minitickets-dev-public-rt
components.city: The road sign on the main road
components.what: Two lines: 10.0.0.0/16 → local (stay inside the city) and 0.0.0.0/0 → igw (everything else: out through the gate).
components.why: This one line, 0.0.0.0/0 → igw, is what makes public-1 and public-2 public.
settings: routes: 0.0.0.0/0 → minitickets-dev-igw
10.0.0.0/16 → local, added by AWS

tours.title: Chapter 0: The app on my laptop

steps.title: 1. Locate web container (Next.js)
explain: It is the part visitors see. On AWS it becomes a worker, kept on shift by a manager.
Builds the pages. Port 3000 inside the container; your browser opens localhost:3100 (pnpm app:up).

console.question: Which setting proves this boundary is configured, and which separate boundary could still fail?

steps.title: 2. Follow api container (Fastify + tRPC)
explain: All server logic lives here. On AWS it becomes a worker in a public neighborhood, guarded so only the reception desk can call it.
Holds the rules and talks to Postgres and Redis. Port 4000 inside, localhost:4100 outside.

console.path: Docker Desktop → Containers → api → Logs
console.question: Which setting proves this boundary is configured, and which separate boundary could still fail?

steps.title: 3. Follow migrate container
